claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–M.

claims.claim: Activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons triggered similar behavioral changes in the backgrounds of +/+, +/fru4-40, or fruM/fru4-40 males.
claims.source: Consistent with this, the activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons triggered similar behavioral changes in the backgrounds of +/+, +/fru4-40, or fruM/fru4-40 males (Figure 1—figure supplement 2N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2N.

claims.claim: Heterozygosity of fruM resulted in incomplete specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in a chromosomally female background.
claims.source: However, heterozygosity of fruM resulted in incomplete specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in a chromosomally female background (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claims.claim: fruFLP is a hypomorphic allele.
claims.source: We also found that fruFLP, a knock-in allele of fru that expresses a DNA recombinase Flippase (Yu et al., 2010), is hypomorphic (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E), raising the necessity to use caution when attempting to transform Drosophila sex by manipulating the fru locus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E and citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruM females induced lunges toward a fruF male target for the majority of testers.
claims.source: Optogenetic activation of the Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruM females induced lunges toward a fruF male target for the majority of testers (Figure 2A2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2; see also Video 4 – Part 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruM females increased orienting time during LED stimulations compared to during inter-stimulus intervals.
claims.source: Although orienting time increased during LED stimulations compared to during ISIs (Figure 2A1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1), no overall change in the amount of wing extensions was observed compared to genetic controls (Figure 2A3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1.

claims.claim: No overall change in the amount of wing extensions was observed in fruM females compared to genetic controls after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons.
claims.source: Although orienting time increased during LED stimulations compared to during ISIs (Figure 2A1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1), no overall change in the amount of wing extensions was observed compared to genetic controls (Figure 2A3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A3.

claims.claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are part of a fruM-dependent, but dsx-independent, neuronal circuit for male-type aggressive behavior.
claims.source: This indicates that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are part of a fruM-dependent, but dsx-independent, neuronal circuit for male-type aggressive behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fruM females (which lack dsxM) can perform lunges when Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are activated.

claims.claim: The motion sequence underlying the lunges observed in fruM females were indistinguishable from wild-type male lunges.
claims.source: The motion sequence underlying the lunges observed in this genotype were indistinguishable from wild-type male lunges (Video 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by video evidence shown in Video 5.

claims.claim: Forty-two percent of fruM females did not perform a single lunge after LED stimulation.
claims.source: Forty-two percent (17/40) of fruM females did not perform a single lunge after LED stimulation (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Over 96% of male testers lunged toward a male target after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, over 96% of male testers lunged toward a male target (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The median of induced lunges observed in fruM females (2) was lower than observed for male testers (58).
claims.source: The median of induced lunges observed in fruM females (2) was lower than observed for male testers (58).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of behavioral data.

claims.claim: fruM females occasionally lunged toward a female target after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons.
claims.source: Second, fruM females occasionally lunged toward a female target (Video 4 – Part 2), in addition to a fruF male target.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by video evidence shown in Video 4 – Part 2.

claims.claim: Male testers seldom lunge toward a female target after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41 neurons.
claims.source: Even though lunges were induced even less frequently than toward fruF males (Figure 2A2, B2, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2, 2B2), it is still noteworthy because male testers seldom lunge toward a female target, even after optogenetic activation of the Tk-GAL41 neurons (Figure 1D2, Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D2 and Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in single-housed fruM females failed to induce a single lunge toward fruF male targets.
claims.source: Interestingly, optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in single-housed fruM females failed to induce a single lunge toward fruF male targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C2 F2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C2 F2.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in single-housed fruM females resulted in higher levels of orientation and wing extensions than exhibited by group-housed flies.
claims.source: Instead, this manipulation resulted in higher levels of orientation and wing extensions than was exhibited by group-housed flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C1, C3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C1, C3.

claims.claim: The relatively high levels of courtship behavior seen in fruM females interferes with the aggression-promoting function of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: These data suggest that the relatively high levels of courtship behavior seen in fruM females interferes with the aggression-promoting function of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that single-housed fruM females (which show more courtship) do not lunge after optogenetic activation.

claims.claim: Group-housed fruM females that did not lunge toward a target fly after optogenetic stimulation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons tended to show higher levels of wing extensions than testers who lunged.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, group-housed fruM females that did not lunge toward a target fly after optogenetic stimulation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons tended to show higher levels of wing extensions than testers who lunged (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E, F1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E, F1.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons did not induce headbutts in fruM females.
claims.source: Lastly, optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons did not induce headbutts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A3, B3), confirming that this genotype is using a male-type aggressive action exclusively (Vrontou et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A3, B3 and citation to Vrontou et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges even in the absence of dsx-dependent aggression-promoting neurons.
claims.source: The activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges even in the absence of dsx-dependent aggression-promoting neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fruM females (which lack male-type dsx-dependent neurons) can perform lunges when Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are activated.

claims.claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are part of a fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male aggressive behavior.
claims.source: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are therefore part of a fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male aggressive behavior (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data presented.

claims.claim: A dsx-dependent mechanism may play a role in establishing a target sex-selective application of aggressive behavior.
claims.source: However, the reduced intensity and compromised target sex selectivity of lunges shown by fruM females suggest that a dsx-dependent mechanism may play a role in establishing a target sex-selective application of aggressive behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fruM females show less selective aggression toward female targets compared to males.

claims.claim: dsx can inhibit the execution of lunges specifically toward females.
claims.source: This mechanism can inhibit the execution of lunges specifically toward females, which ensures that lunges are performed exclusively by males towards other males (Figure 2D), or can enhance aggression specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship toward them.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism by which dsx affects target sex selectivity.

claims.claim: dsx can enhance aggression specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship toward them.
claims.source: This mechanism can inhibit the execution of lunges specifically toward females, which ensures that lunges are performed exclusively by males towards other males (Figure 2D), or can enhance aggression specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship toward them.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism by which dsx affects target sex selectivity.

claims.claim: dsx specifies the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
claims.source: As was discussed above, dsx specifies the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, such that the morphology of these neurons in fruM females is largely female-type, and not male-type (Figure 3A; see also Ishii et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Ishii et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The morphology of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females is largely female-type, and not male-type.
claims.source: As was discussed above, dsx specifies the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, such that the morphology of these neurons in fruM females is largely female-type, and not male-type (Figure 3A; see also Ishii et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Ishii et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased time orienting toward female target flies.
claims.source: We confirmed that optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased time orienting (Figure 3C1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B1) and headbutts (Figure 3C2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B2) toward female target flies, mostly during LED stimulation (see also Video 6 – Part 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B1.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased headbutts toward female target flies.
claims.source: We confirmed that optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased time orienting (Figure 3C1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B1) and headbutts (Figure 3C2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B2) toward female target flies, mostly during LED stimulation (see also Video 6 – Part 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B2.

claims.claim: The behavioral phenotype of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neuron activation was consistently observed when the fru locus was either +/+, +/fru4-40 or fruF/fru4-40.
claims.source: This behavioral phenotype was consistently observed when the fru locus was either +/+, +/fru4-40 or fruF/fru4-40, similar to the case in males (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females induced similar behaviors toward fruF male targets as toward female targets.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed similar behaviors toward the fruF male targets as well (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; see also Video 6 – Part 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons did not overlap with neurons labeled by the R71G01-LexA transgene.
claims.source: However, we found that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons did not overlap with neurons labeled by the R71G01-LexA transgene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claims.claim: Female 'pC1' neurons are anatomically and functionally heterogeneous.
claims.source: This is consistent with recent findings that female 'pC1' neurons are anatomically and functionally heterogeneous (Deutsch et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2020, and Wu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females did not induce lunges or headbutts.
claims.source: Interestingly, we did not observe induction of either lunges or headbutts (Figure 3D2 and E2,3) when we optogenetically activated the NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D2 and E2,3.

claims.claim: Female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons can promote headbutts only if other mechanisms that rely on sexually dimorphic splicing of fru are present in the brain.
claims.source: Thus, female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons can promote headbutts only if other mechanisms that rely on sexually dimorphic splicing of fru are present in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote headbutts in fruM females.

claims.claim: Female-like NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons fail to establish functional connections with neurons that are part of the fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male-type aggression.
claims.source: In addition, this result suggests that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons with female-like morphology fail to establish functional connections with neurons that are part of the fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male-type aggression (which includes Tk-GAL4FruM neurons; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claims.claim: Female-like NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot participate in generation of aggressive behavior without separate populations of neurons that are specified in the absence of fruM.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that female-like NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot participate in generation of aggressive behavior (e.g. headbutts) without separate populations of neurons that are specified in the absence of fruM.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claims.claim: The sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons does not determine the sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions.
claims.source: This finding raises a possibility that the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, which is largely specified by dsx, does not determine the sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claims.claim: Male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot trigger lunges without a fruM-dependent mechanism.
claims.source: As is shown in Ishii et al. (2020), male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot trigger lunges without a fruM-dependent mechanism, underscoring the dominant role of fru and fru-dependent neural circuits in specifying sexually dimorphic action patterns during aggressive interactions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2020.

claims.claim: fru has a dominant role in specifying sexually dimorphic action patterns during aggressive interactions.
claims.source: As is shown in Ishii et al. (2020), male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot trigger lunges without a fruM-dependent mechanism, underscoring the dominant role of fru and fru-dependent neural circuits in specifying sexually dimorphic action patterns during aggressive interactions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons require fruM-dependent mechanisms to trigger lunges.

claims.claim: fruM undergoes alternative splicing to create three transcript isoforms: fruMA, fruMB, and fruMC.
claims.source: fruM undergoes another layer of alternative splicing to create three transcript isoforms, fruMA, fruMB, and fruMC, (Figure 4A), which encode different zinc finger domains (Usui-Aoki et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Usui-Aoki et al., 2000 and schematic shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The three fruM isoforms encode different zinc finger domains.
claims.source: fruM undergoes another layer of alternative splicing to create three transcript isoforms, fruMA, fruMB, and fruMC, (Figure 4A), which encode different zinc finger domains (Usui-Aoki et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Usui-Aoki et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The loss of each of three fruM isoforms affects male courtship behaviors in distinct manners.
claims.source: The loss of each of three fruM isoforms is known to affect male courtship behaviors in distinct manners (Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neville et al., 2014 and von Philipsborn et al., 2014, as well as data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Loss of fruMA caused no reduction of lunges compared to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control.
claims.source: Loss of fruMA caused no reduction of lunges compared to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control (Figure 4B2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B2.

claims.claim: Loss of fruMB caused a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors.
claims.source: In contrast, we observed a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors by the loss of fruMB or fruMC isoforms (Figure 4B2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B2.

claims.claim: Loss of fruMC caused a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors.
claims.source: In contrast, we observed a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors by the loss of fruMB or fruMC isoforms (Figure 4B2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B2.

claims.claim: fruMC mutants showed decreased orientation time toward a male target.
claims.source: While fruMC mutants showed decreased orientation time toward a male target, orienting times of fruMA and fruMB mutants were comparable to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control (Figure 4A1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A1 (note: the text says 4A1 but likely means 4B1).

claims.claim: Orienting times of fruMA and fruMB mutants were comparable to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control.
claims.source: While fruMC mutants showed decreased orientation time toward a male target, orienting times of fruMA and fruMB mutants were comparable to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control (Figure 4A1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A1 (note: the text says 4A1 but likely means 4B1).

claims.claim: The reduction in lunges in fruMB mutants was qualitatively recapitulated when the fruF allele was used to create trans-heterozygotes.
claims.source: This reduction in lunges in fruMB mutants was qualitatively recapitulated when the fruF allele was used to create trans-heterozygotes (Figure 4C), and when other mutations affecting FruB zinc finger domains (von Philipsborn et al., 2014) were tested in trans with fru4-40 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, as well as citation to von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claims.claim: No consistent reduction in overall activity levels was observed between fruMB mutants and genetic controls.
claims.source: We observed no consistent reduction in overall activity levels between fruMB mutants and genetic controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), or in the total amount of sleep exhibited by these flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by activity data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: No consistent reduction in the total amount of sleep was observed between fruMB mutants and genetic controls.
claims.source: We observed no consistent reduction in overall activity levels between fruMB mutants and genetic controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), or in the total amount of sleep exhibited by these flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Male-male courtship was differentially affected in the three fruM isoform mutants.
claims.source: Male-male courtship was differentially affected in three mutants (Figure 4A3), reflecting varied degrees of courtship defects toward females (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B; Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A3 (note: likely means 4B3), Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, and citations to Neville et al., 2014 and von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Each of the three fruM isoforms make different contributions to aggressive behaviors.
claims.source: These data indicate that each of the three fruM isoforms make different contributions to aggressive behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of fruM isoform mutations on aggressive behavior.

claims.claim: fruMA had a minimal impact on male aggressive behavior.
claims.source: fruMA had a minimal impact on male aggressive behavior, whereas fruMB and fruMC were both necessary to maintain normal levels of male aggression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing no reduction in lunges in fruMA mutants.

claims.claim: fruMB and fruMC were both necessary to maintain normal levels of male aggression.
claims.source: fruMA had a minimal impact on male aggressive behavior, whereas fruMB and fruMC were both necessary to maintain normal levels of male aggression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing reduced lunges in fruMB and fruMC mutants.

claims.claim: The decreased aggression of fruMB mutants was not necessarily due to reduced activity levels or opportunities to interact with the target fly.
claims.source: Moreover, the decreased aggression of fruMB mutants was not necessarily due to reduced activity levels or opportunities to interact with the target fly.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fruMB mutants show normal activity levels and orienting time.

claims.claim: In fruMC mutants, only 1.9 ± 1.1 faintly labeled neurons were found in the brain area where Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are expected to appear.
claims.source: In fruMC mutants, we found only 1.9 ± 1.1 (mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5D,E) faintly labeled neurons in the brain area where Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are expected to appear, significantly fewer than the number of cells found in genetic controls (5.6 ± 0.5, mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5A,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative anatomical data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claims.claim: The number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMC mutants was significantly fewer than in genetic controls.
claims.source: In fruMC mutants, we found only 1.9 ± 1.1 (mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5D,E) faintly labeled neurons in the brain area where Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are expected to appear, significantly fewer than the number of cells found in genetic controls (5.6 ± 0.5, mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5A,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative anatomical data shown in Figure 5A,E.

claims.claim: fruMA and fruMB mutants did not affect the number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, fruMA and fruMB mutants did not affect the number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative anatomical data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from fruMA or fruMB mutants are indistinguishable from each other or from fru4-40 heterozygous control males.
claims.source: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from fruMA (Figure 5G) or fruMB (Figure 5H) mutants are indistinguishable from each other or from fru4-40 heterozygous control males (Figure 5F; see also Video 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by registered and averaged imaging data shown in Figure 5F-H and Video 7.

claims.claim: No significant differences in volumes of three prominent neurites of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons were detected among fru4-40 heterozygous controls, fruMA mutants, and fruMB mutants.
claims.source: We measured the volumes of three prominent neurites that emanate from the lateral junction (Yu et al., 2010) of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 5F2–H2; see also Figure 1L1, M1), and detected no significant differences among fru4-40 heterozygous controls, fruMA mutants, and fruMB mutants (Figure 5I–K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative volume measurements shown in Figure 5I–K and citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Heterozygosity of all isoform-specific mutations did not change the cell body number or gross morphology of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: Heterozygosity of all isoform-specific mutations did not change the cell body number or gross morphology of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D), either.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claims.claim: fruMA, fruMB and fruMC have distinct effects on male aggression and specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: Taken together, we found that fruMA, fruMB and fruMC have distinct effects on male aggression and specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruM isoform mutants.

claims.claim: fruMA appeared largely dispensable for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: fruMA appeared largely dispensable for both, whereas fruMC was necessary for both.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMA mutants.

claims.claim: fruMC was necessary for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: fruMA appeared largely dispensable for both, whereas fruMC was necessary for both.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMC mutants.

claims.claim: fruMB was necessary for normal levels of male-male aggression, but was not required for specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, fruMB was necessary for normal levels of male-male aggression, but was not required for specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMB mutants.

claims.claim: The overall calcium response dynamics and magnitudes of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants were comparable to those seen in the fru4-40 heterozygous controls.
claims.source: The overall calcium response dynamics and magnitudes of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants were comparable to those seen in the fru4-40 heterozygous controls (Figure 6C,D), suggesting that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants are capable of physiologically responding to depolarizing stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claims.claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants are capable of physiologically responding to depolarizing stimuli.
claims.source: The overall calcium response dynamics and magnitudes of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants were comparable to those seen in the fru4-40 heterozygous controls (Figure 6C,D), suggesting that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants are capable of physiologically responding to depolarizing stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing normal responses in fruMB mutants.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruMB mutants elicited robust levels of male aggression across several LED intensities.
claims.source: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruMB mutants elicited robust levels of male aggression across several LED intensities, as seen in genetic controls (Figure 6E–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants, once activated, can induce male aggression as efficiently as in the fru wild-type males.
claims.source: This result suggests that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants, once activated, can induce male aggression as efficiently as in the fru wild-type males, and argues against the hypothesis that the mutation of fruMB proteins causes defective development of downstream neurons or reduced efficiency of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons to excite downstream neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants induces normal levels of aggression.

claims.claim: fruMB mutation reduces aggression-promoting input to Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from upstream circuits.
claims.source: Instead, these results favor the alternative hypothesis that fruMB mutation reduces aggression-promoting input to Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from upstream circuits.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that fruMB mutants show reduced spontaneous aggression but normal aggression when Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are optogenetically activated.

claims.claim: Three isoforms of fruM assume distinct roles in the specification and function of sexually dimorphic neurons that control male-type aggressive behaviors.
claims.source: Overall, our results show that three isoforms of fruM assume distinct roles in the specification and function of sexually dimorphic neurons that control male-type aggressive behaviors (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral, anatomical, and functional data on fruM isoform mutants.

claims.claim: fruMC is necessary for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: Namely, fruMC is necessary for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, whereas fruMB is necessary for a normal level of spontaneous aggression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical data showing reduced Tk-GAL4FruM neuron numbers in fruMC mutants.

claims.claim: fruMB is necessary for a normal level of spontaneous aggression.
claims.source: Namely, fruMC is necessary for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, whereas fruMB is necessary for a normal level of spontaneous aggression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing reduced spontaneous aggression in fruMB mutants.

claims.claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and downstream populations form a neural circuit that is sufficient for the execution of male-type aggressive behavior.
claims.source: We found that the optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruM female tester flies induced male-type aggressive behavior. This result indicates that at least Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and downstream populations form a neural circuit that is sufficient for the execution of male-type aggressive behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruM females induces lunges.

claims.claim: Neurons specified by fru form the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive action.
claims.source: These observations favor a hypothesis that neurons specified by fru, which include Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, form the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive action, and NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons serve as modulatory neurons that act on this fru-dependent execution mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (specified by fru) can induce lunges in fruM females.

claims.claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons serve as modulatory neurons that act on the fru-dependent execution mechanism.
claims.source: These observations favor a hypothesis that neurons specified by fru, which include Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, form the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive action, and NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons serve as modulatory neurons that act on this fru-dependent execution mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not induce aggression in fruM females.

claims.claim: Sex-specific splicing of fru defines what type of aggressive behavior an animal performs.
claims.source: Sex-specific splicing of fru defines what type of aggressive behavior an animal performs, likely by specifying a mutually exclusive neural circuit that generates either male-type or female-type aggressive actions.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that fruM females perform male-type aggression.

claims.claim: dsx is important for suppressing inappropriate aggressive behavior toward a female target.
claims.source: In fact, fruM females lunge against females as well as fruF males, suggesting that dsx is important for suppressing inappropriate aggressive behavior toward a female target.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fruM females (which lack dsxM) lunge toward female targets.

claims.claim: dsx-expressing neurons respond to sex-specific sensory cues, such as olfactory, gustatory, and auditory stimuli.
claims.source: Intriguingly, however, dsx-expressing neurons respond to sex-specific sensory cues, such as olfactory, gustatory, and auditory stimuli (Deutsch et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2019, Zhou et al., 2014, and Zhou et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Thermogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges toward a male target that lacks cuticular hydrocarbons.
claims.source: Since thermogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges toward a male target that lacks cuticular hydrocarbons (Asahina et al., 2014), one possible scenario is that a dsx-dependent circuit is responsible for detection or transmission of female-specific, aggression-suppressing cues that have yet to be identified.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Asahina et al., 2014.

claims.claim: A dsx-dependent circuit may be responsible for detection or transmission of female-specific, aggression-suppressing cues.
claims.source: Since thermogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges toward a male target that lacks cuticular hydrocarbons (Asahina et al., 2014), one possible scenario is that a dsx-dependent circuit is responsible for detection or transmission of female-specific, aggression-suppressing cues that have yet to be identified.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of dsx in target sex selectivity.

claims.claim: dsx in males may allow execution of male-type aggressive behavior specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship behavior toward males.
claims.source: Alternatively, dsx in males may allow execution of male-type aggressive behavior specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship behavior toward males.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of dsx in target sex selectivity.

claims.claim: Courtship behavior can interfere with aggressive behavior, possibly through feedforward inhibitory circuits.
claims.source: fruM females that showed high levels of courtship behavior generally showed low levels of male-type aggression. This observation suggests that courtship behavior can interfere with aggressive behavior, possibly through feedforward inhibitory circuits (Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Koganezawa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fruM females with high courtship show low aggression, supported by citations to Clowney et al., 2015, Kallman et al., 2015, and Koganezawa et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Information about target sex can be supplied downstream of Tk-GAL4FruM neuronal activities and modify its behavioral influence.
claims.source: The contribution of dsx on the target sex-selective execution of aggressive behavior also implies that information about target sex can be supplied downstream of Tk-GAL4FruM neuronal activities and modify its behavioral influence.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dsx affects target sex selectivity of aggression.

claims.claim: dsx-specified neurons may serve as a 'block' against neuronal activity generated by Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and other unidentified constituents of the lunge execution mechanism.
claims.source: It is possible that dsx-specified neurons serve as a 'block' against neuronal activity generated by Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and other unidentified constituents of the lunge execution mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism by which dsx affects target sex selectivity.

claims.claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females promote female-type aggression.
claims.source: Consistent with a previous observation (Koganezawa et al., 2016), we observed that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females promote female-type aggression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and citation to Koganezawa et al., 2016.

claims.claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons belong to a cluster of dsx-expressing 'pC1' neurons.
claims.source: This population belongs to a cluster of dsx-expressing 'pC1' neurons, which is known to promote a variety of female social behaviors including aggression (Deutsch et al., 2020; Palavicino-Maggio et al., 2019; Robie et al., 2017), receptivity (Deutsch et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014) or even courtship-like behaviors (Rezával et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2020, Palavicino-Maggio et al., 2019, Robie et al., 2017, Zhou et al., 2014, Rezával et al., 2016, and Wu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: 'pC1' neurons promote a variety of female social behaviors including aggression, receptivity, and courtship-like behaviors.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2020, Palavicino-Maggio et al., 2019, Robie et al., 2017, Zhou et al., 2014, Rezával et al., 2016, and Wu et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are unlikely to be a part of the execution mechanism that generates female-type aggressive actions.
claims.source: In spite of the importance of 'pC1' neurons collectively on female social behaviors, female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are unlikely to be a part of the execution mechanism that generates female-type aggressive actions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claims.claim: There are uncharacterized sexually dimorphic neurons that are necessary for females to execute headbutts and other female-specific aggressive actions.
claims.source: Our results suggest that there are uncharacterized sexually dimorphic neurons that are necessary for females to execute headbutts and other female-specific aggressive actions, likely downstream of female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claims.claim: fruMC is important for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
claims.source: Our result is in line with the previously reported importance of the fruMC isoform in the development of male-specific branching patterns in several fruM-expressing neurons (Billeter et al., 2006; Ito et al., 2016; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Billeter et al., 2006, Ito et al., 2016, and von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claims.claim: fruMC is necessary for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons at behavioral and circuitry levels.
claims.source: Our observation that fruMC is necessary for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons reveals its importance for male-type aggressive behavior as well, at behavioral and circuitry levels.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMC mutants.

claims.claim: fruMC can be regarded as exerting 'organizational' functions.
claims.source: Using an analogy from the function of steroid hormones in mammals (McCarthy, 2008), fruMC can be regarded as exerting 'organizational' functions, while fruMB may exert 'activation' functions, in the sense that fruMB is dispensable for the specification of a lunge execution mechanism, yet is necessary for induction of spontaneous aggressive behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is an analogy drawn from mammalian steroid hormone function, supported by citation to McCarthy, 2008.

claims.evidence: This is an analogy drawn from mammalian steroid hormone function, supported by citation to McCarthy, 2008.

claims.source: The segregation of roles within fru isoforms may increase the gene's flexibility: for instance, change in the circuit connectivity underlying perception of male-specific cues can be independently altered if different isoforms have different roles in the aggression circuit.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the evolutionary implications of fru isoform diversity.

claims.claim: There are at least 3 different estrogen receptor genes in mice.

claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the function of estrogen receptor genes in mice.

claims.source: Our results suggest that one of the reasons behind this apparent genetic cooperativity may be that each gene controls specific aspects of sexually dimorphic traits, including behaviors (Pereira et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential roles of dsx and fru, supported by citations to Pereira et al., 2019 and Xu et al., 2012.

claims.source: The dsx gene produces functional proteins in both sexes, and mediates specification of not only male-type circuits for courtship but also female-type circuits that make females receptive to such motor programs (Deutsch et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2014.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2002, Nilsen et al., 2004, and Smith and Price, 1973.

claims.claim: Sexually dimorphic traits that bring advantage specifically during inter-male competition can be fixed through evolution even if it is not directly under sexual selection.
claims.source: Consequently, aggressive actions can be under a different selection pressure from courtship behavior. Ample examples of male-specific weaponry organs across a variety of species support the hypothesis that sexually dimorphic traits that bring advantage specifically during inter-male competition can be fixed through evolution even if it is not directly under sexual selection (Rico-Guevara and Hurme, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Rico-Guevara and Hurme, 2018.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fru is important for aggression but not for certain aspects of courtship, supported by citations to Davis et al., 2000 and Ishii et al., 2020.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shirangi et al., 2009.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in males induces robust aggression (lunges) toward male targets during LED stimulation, increases orienting time toward both male and female targets, but does not induce lunges toward female targets or in the absence of a target. Wing extension toward males is not affected, while wing extension toward females is reduced during stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C10 are well-supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures (Figure 1C-D, supplementary figures, and videos). The behavioral phenotypes are consistently observed across different stimulation frequencies and genetic backgrounds. Statistical tests confirm significant differences between experimental and control groups. The claim that lunges occur strictly when a male target is present (C10) is a logical inference from the data showing no lunges with female targets or without targets.

results.result: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are specified predominantly by fru and not by dsx. These neurons are present in males and fruM females but not in fruF males. The cell body number and morphology (including volumes of three prominent neurite processes) are indistinguishable between males and fruM females. FruM protein is expressed in these neurons while Dsx protein is not.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C27 are strongly supported by anatomical data including immunohistochemistry (Figure 1G-M, supplementary figures), cell counts (Figure 1K), and volumetric measurements (Figure 1N-P). The morphological analysis using registration and segmentation is rigorous, though the authors acknowledge potential limitations in detecting finer-scale differences. Statistical tests show no significant differences in cell number or neurite volumes between males and fruM females. The conclusion that dsx and fru have separable roles (C27) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruM females induces male-type aggressive behavior (lunges) toward male targets, demonstrating that these neurons are part of a fruM-dependent, but dsx-independent, execution mechanism for male-type aggression. However, the induction is less consistent and intense than in males (42% of fruM females did not lunge vs. >96% of males lunging), and fruM females occasionally lunge toward female targets, unlike males.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C48 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 2A-C, supplementary figures, and videos). The key finding that fruM females can perform male-type lunges when Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are activated is well-documented. Statistical tests confirm significant differences between experimental and control groups. The reduced consistency and intensity compared to males, and the occasional lunges toward females, are quantitatively documented. The conclusion that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are part of a fruM-dependent execution mechanism (C48) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: Single-housed fruM females fail to lunge after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, instead showing higher levels of orientation and wing extensions than group-housed flies. This suggests that high levels of courtship behavior in fruM females interfere with the aggression-promoting function of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C, E, F). The observation that single-housed fruM females (which show more courtship) do not lunge is well-documented. The inference that courtship interferes with aggression (C44) is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat speculative. The correlation between high wing extension and lack of lunging (C45) provides additional support for this interpretation.

results.result: A dsx-dependent mechanism may play a role in establishing target sex-selective application of aggressive behavior, either by inhibiting lunges specifically toward females or by enhancing aggression toward male targets indirectly through inhibiting courtship toward males.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are speculative hypotheses based on the observation that fruM females show reduced target sex selectivity. While the data support the idea that dsx affects target selectivity, the specific mechanisms proposed (C50, C51) are not directly tested. These claims represent reasonable interpretations but require additional experiments to distinguish between the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: dsx specifies the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons such that their morphology in fruM females is female-type. Optogenetic activation of these neurons in females robustly increases orienting and headbutts toward both female and male targets, consistently across different fru genotypes. These neurons do not overlap with R71G01-LexA labeled neurons, consistent with heterogeneity of female 'pC1' neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C59 are supported by anatomical data (Figure 3A, supplementary figures) and behavioral data (Figure 3B-C, supplementary figures). The morphological characterization is based on prior work (Ishii et al., 2020) and current observations. The behavioral phenotypes are consistently observed across different fru genotypes. The lack of overlap with R71G01-LexA neurons is documented anatomically. The conclusion about heterogeneity of pC1 neurons (C59) is supported by multiple citations.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females does not induce lunges or headbutts, suggesting that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons can only promote headbutts if other fru-dependent mechanisms are present, and that they fail to establish functional connections with the fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male-type aggression. This raises the possibility that the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons does not determine the sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 3D-E). The lack of aggression induction in fruM females is well-documented. The inferences about functional connectivity (C62) and the role of sexual dimorphism (C64) are reasonable given the data, though C64 is somewhat speculative. The conclusion that female-like NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot participate in aggression without separate fru-dependent neurons (C63) is well-justified.

results.result: The three fruM isoforms (fruMA, fruMB, fruMC) have distinct effects on male aggressive behavior. Loss of fruMA has minimal impact on aggression, while loss of fruMB or fruMC causes dramatic reductions in lunges. fruMC mutants also show decreased orientation time. The reduction in aggression in fruMB mutants is not due to reduced activity levels or sleep. Male-male courtship is differentially affected in the three mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C82 are well-supported by behavioral data (Figure 4B-C, supplementary figures) and prior literature. The differential effects of the three isoforms on aggression are clearly documented with appropriate statistical tests. The control experiments showing normal activity and sleep in fruMB mutants (C76, C77) strengthen the conclusion that the aggression defect is specific. The conclusion that each isoform makes different contributions (C79) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: fruMC is necessary for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (only 1.9 ± 1.1 faintly labeled neurons in fruMC mutants vs. 5.6 ± 0.5 in controls), while fruMA and fruMB mutants have normal numbers of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons with indistinguishable morphology. Interestingly, fruMB is necessary for normal levels of male-male aggression but not for specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C92 are strongly supported by anatomical data including cell counts (Figure 5E), registered and averaged images (Figure 5F-H), and volumetric measurements (Figure 5I-K). The quantitative data clearly show that fruMC affects neuron specification while fruMB does not. Statistical tests confirm significant differences. The conclusion that the three isoforms have distinct effects (C89) is well-justified. The finding that fruMB is necessary for behavior but not neuron specification (C92) is a key result.

results.result: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants show normal calcium response dynamics and magnitudes, and optogenetic activation of these neurons elicits robust aggression comparable to controls. This suggests that fruMB mutation reduces aggression-promoting input to Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from upstream circuits rather than affecting the neurons themselves or their downstream targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 6C-D) and behavioral data (Figure 6E-G). The calcium imaging shows normal responses in fruMB mutants, and the optogenetic activation experiments show normal aggression induction. The inference that fruMB affects upstream inputs (C97) is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat speculative. The conclusion that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants can induce aggression as efficiently as in wild-type (C96) is well-supported.

results.result: The three isoforms of fruM assume distinct roles in the specification and function of sexually dimorphic neurons controlling male-type aggressive behaviors. Specifically, fruMC is necessary for specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, while fruMB is necessary for normal levels of spontaneous aggression.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are well-supported by the combined behavioral, anatomical, and functional data presented in Figures 4-6. The distinct roles of fruMC (specification) and fruMB (function) are clearly documented. This is a major conclusion of the paper that integrates multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and downstream populations form a neural circuit sufficient for execution of male-type aggressive behavior. Neurons specified by fru form the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive action, while NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons serve as modulatory neurons. Sex-specific splicing of fru defines what type of aggressive behavior an animal performs. dsx is important for suppressing inappropriate aggressive behavior toward female targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 are supported by the behavioral data from fruM females and the comparison with NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neuron manipulations. The conclusion that fru-specified neurons form the execution mechanism (C102) is a reasonable inference from the data. The role of dsx in target sex selectivity (C105) is supported by the observation that fruM females lunge toward females. Claims C103 and C104 are somewhat speculative but reasonable given the data.

results.result: Prior work has established that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are male-specific fru-expressing neurons that promote and are necessary for male aggression, that fruM females show male-type aggression, and that fru is the chief architect of neural circuits underlying sexual dimorphism in aggressive behavior. However, not all fru-expressing neurons underlie sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions, as some (like male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP and P1a neurons) are not specified in fruM females. Male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot trigger lunges without a fruM-dependent mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14-C18, C65-C66 are all supported by citations to prior published work (Asahina et al., 2014; Vrontou et al., 2006; Koganezawa et al., 2016; Hoopfer et al., 2015; Ishii et al., 2020). These claims establish the context and prior knowledge for the current study. The inference that not all fru-expressing neurons underlie sexual dimorphism (C18) is reasonable given the cited evidence.

results.result: The fru4-40 allele does not affect cell number or morphology of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, and activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons triggers similar behavioral changes in +/+, +/fru4-40, or fruM/fru4-40 males. However, heterozygosity of fruM results in incomplete specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in females, and fruFLP is a hypomorphic allele.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by anatomical data (Figure 1K, supplementary figures) and behavioral data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2N). The finding that fru4-40 does not affect Tk-GAL4FruM neurons is important for interpreting the isoform-specific mutant experiments. The observation that fruFLP is hypomorphic (C31) is a useful technical note supported by data.

results.result: dsx-expressing neurons respond to sex-specific sensory cues. Thermogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges toward male targets lacking cuticular hydrocarbons, suggesting a dsx-dependent circuit may be responsible for detecting female-specific aggression-suppressing cues. Alternatively, dsx may allow execution of male-type aggression toward males by inhibiting courtship toward males. Courtship behavior can interfere with aggressive behavior, possibly through feedforward inhibitory circuits. Information about target sex can be supplied downstream of Tk-GAL4FruM neuronal activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C112 mix well-supported observations (C106, C107, C110 supported by citations and data) with speculative hypotheses about mechanisms (C108, C109, C112). The proposed mechanisms for how dsx affects target sex selectivity are reasonable but not directly tested. These claims represent important discussion points but require additional experiments for full validation.

results.result: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females promote female-type aggression and belong to the dsx-expressing 'pC1' neuron cluster, which promotes various female social behaviors. However, female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are unlikely to be part of the execution mechanism for female-type aggressive actions. There are likely uncharacterized sexually dimorphic neurons necessary for females to execute headbutts and other female-specific aggressive actions.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by behavioral data and multiple citations to prior work. The conclusion that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are not part of the execution mechanism (C116) is based on the observation that they don't promote aggression in fruM females. The speculation about uncharacterized neurons (C117) is reasonable given the data but remains to be tested.

results.result: fruMC is important for specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and development of male-specific branching patterns in several fruM-expressing neurons, consistent with prior work. fruMC is necessary for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons at behavioral and circuitry levels. Using an analogy from mammalian steroid hormones, fruMC can be regarded as exerting 'organizational' functions while fruMB may exert 'activation' functions. The segregation of roles within fru isoforms may increase the gene's flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C126 are supported by the current data and citations to prior work. The analogy to mammalian steroid hormones (C124-C125) is reasonable and supported by citation to McCarthy, 2008. The speculation about evolutionary flexibility (C126) is reasonable but remains speculative. The main conclusions about fruMC's organizational role are well-supported.

results.result: There are at least 3 different estrogen receptor genes in mice, and a similar division of labor may exist among them. Each sex-determining gene controls specific aspects of sexually dimorphic traits, including behaviors. Separate genetic mechanisms for establishing sexually dimorphic actions and target sex-dependent action bias may be evolutionarily adaptive.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 are largely speculative, drawing parallels between Drosophila and mammalian systems. C127 is supported by citation, but C128 is explicitly speculative. C129 is a reasonable conclusion from the current work supported by citations. C130 is speculative about evolutionary implications. These claims represent interesting discussion points but are not directly tested.

results.result: dsx plays an important role in specifying the male courtship execution circuit and produces functional proteins in both sexes, mediating specification of both male-type and female-type circuits. This dual function may ensure species-specificity of courtship rituals during speciation. In contrast, aggressive behavior is executed by sexually dimorphic motor programs often between same-sex individuals. fru is well-situated to be a genetic agent for male-specific modification of aggressive behavior, while dsx can ensure males do not act aggressively toward females. Female-type somatic characteristics, including sex-specific chemical cues, are specified by dsx.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C142 are supported by citations to prior work and represent the broader context and implications of the current findings. The claims about dsx function in courtship (C131-C135) are well-supported by citations. The claims about aggressive behavior (C136-C137) are supported by citations. The evolutionary arguments (C138-C140) are supported by citations and represent reasonable interpretations. The conclusions about the distinct roles of fru and dsx (C140-C142) are well-supported by the current work and prior literature.
